metas.name: 45° angle transformers
metas.note: Transformers on Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia will be installed at a 45° angle relative to the road. On PEI, red numbers will usually be written on the side.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Alberta bollards
metas.note:
Alberta has a unique black and white bollard that is often found at intersections. It has a cylindrical shape and two black bands that wrap all the way around. It is one of the most useful Canadian bollards to learn because it appears so frequently.

NOTE: Some Alberta bollards have a yellow band between the two black bands, instead of a white one. Blue bands can also rarely be seen, particularly in and around Calgary, while green bands are rarely seen in and around Edmonton.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Alberta license plates
metas.note: Alberta license plates has red text on white background, it shows up as a red tint in the blur. It can be hard to see and it takes some time to get used to spotting it. Front plates are NOT required. Note: New Brunswick has similar license plates.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: British Columbian speed limit signs
metas.note:
Some provinces have unique speed signs.

British Columbian signs include the ‘km/h’ but lack the black section in the Ontario sign.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Concrete barriers
metas.note: British Columbia predominantly uses concrete barriers instead of guardrails.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Exposed rocks
metas.note: The Canadian Shield extends through the eastern part of Canada. Therefore, you will commonly see exposed rocks on street view in the highlighted area.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Green and white striped sticker
metas.note: You can sometimes find a green and white striped sticker on signposts in Manitoba.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Manitoba bollards
metas.note:
Manitoba uses black and grey painted bollards. Most of the time an orange stripe will be present below the grey one.

Wooden, rectangular bollards of this form are typically found further north in Manitoba

NOTE: Bollards in this format with just a black top are seen in Manitoba and Saskatchewan.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Manitoba license plates
metas.note: Manitoba license plates has green on both sides. Front plates are required.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Newfoundland bins
metas.note:
Bins made of wood planks can be seen on Newfoundland driveways. These are most commonly octagonal, however they can have other shapes.

NOTE: Although they are most common in Newfoundland, they can also sometimes be seen in other provinces, such as New Brunswick.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Newfoundland fire hydrant markers
metas.note: Fire hydrants in Newfoundland often have a diamond-shaped marker next to them.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Ontario diamond-shaped markers
metas.note: You can find these diamond-shaped markers on the sides of the roads in Ontario. The colours can vary.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Ontario KM markers
metas.note: Ontario KM markers have a white square at the bottom, which is unique to the province.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Ontario pole tops
metas.note:
These distinctive pole tops are most commonly found in Ontario. They have two insulators to the side, and one on top. The side insulators are affixed to the pole with a distinct attachment. Sometimes, multiple of them can be stacked on top of each other.

NOTE: They can occasionally appear in British Columbia, Nova Scotia, or other provinces more rarely.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Ontario speed limit signs
metas.note:
Some provinces have unique speed signs.

Ontario speed limit signs may have a black section on the bottom with the words ‘km/h’ or ‘begins’ written in white.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Ontario traffic cones
metas.note: Ontario uses distinct orange and black striped traffic cones.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Ontario wooden guardrail posts
metas.note: In Ontario, you will often see these types of guardrails. They consist of cylindrical wooden posts, held together by precisely three metal wires. Some posts are marked by a reflective white band.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Prince Edward Island red soil
metas.note:
Prince Edward Island soil has a distinct red tint to it. Potato farming is also very common on PEI.

NOTE: This type of soil can occasionally be seen in certain areas of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Québec bollards
metas.note: Québec has unique bollards that are always attached to guardrails. They are long, thin white poles with a red or green reflector at the top.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Québec fire hydrant markers
metas.note:
You will often find these yellow fire hydrant markers atop signposts in Québec.

In Québec City these markers will usually have a blue rectangle and markers in Trois-Rivières are distinctly small.

NOTE: Sometimes the markers will have different colours. Beware that Edmundston, in New Brunswick, uses these too.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Québec French speed limit signs
metas.note:
Some provinces have unique speed signs.

Québec can sometimes have French on their speed limit signs.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Québec poles
metas.note: Some Québec poles have recognizable pole tops with insulator rods that are angled slightly upwards.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Québec traffic cones
metas.note: Québec has unique orange and white striped traffic cones.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Saskatchewan alternating insulators
metas.note: Pole top insulators in Saskatchewan alternate. While one pole will have one insulator on the left and two on the right, the next will have two on the left and one on the right.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Saskatchewan license plates
metas.note: Saskatchewan license plates has green text on white background, it shows up as a green tint in the blur. It can be hard to see and it takes some time to get used to spotting it. Front plates are NOT required.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Stop and Arrêt signs
metas.note:
Stop signs with both ‘Stop’ and ‘Arrêt’ are most commonly found in New Brunswick.

NOTE: Such stop signs can rarely be found in other provinces.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Transformers facing the road
metas.note: The transformers on poles will face the road in British Columbia and New Brunswick, while in other provinces, it will be parallel with the wires.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: White triangles on signpost
metas.note: Signposts in Saskatchewan can feature these white triangles. The number can vary.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Wooden post pyramid top
metas.note: In Newfoundland and Labrador, most wooden posts on guardrails have this pyramid shaped top. Occasionally, you can spot them on standalone posts and signposts as well.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.
